tweets.text:
The US goods trade deficit jumped to $149.5B in October, driven by AI imports, far wider than the $135.6B expected and up from a revised $135.1B. That's the widest since March 2025, the third-widest on record and the 4th straight increase. 2026's deficit has now overtaken 2025's record pace.

▪️ Imports +6.1% to a record $365.3B, the biggest jump since January 2025, with all six major categories rising.
▪️ Capital goods imports (computers, chips and telecom gear for the AI buildout) +$13.4B to a record $171.4B, +80.0% from a year ago and up in 11 of the last 12 months.
▪️ That's the fastest growth on record: Q3 capital goods imports were up 59.8% year-over-year, topping the 56.4% of Q4 1972 in data back to 1967.
▪️ The capital goods deficit widened to $95.6B from $36.6B a year ago and accounted for about three-quarters of October's widening.
▪️ Exports were still up 3.2% to $215.8B, the most since April, including a record $75.8B in capital goods, but covered only about a third of the import jump.
▪️ Unlike the March 2025 tariff rush, when consumer goods led ($101.6B vs. $93.1B for capital goods) and the surge reversed within a month, now capital goods dwarf consumer goods ($171.4B vs. $61.4B), and the climb has been steady for more than a year.
▪️ The year-to-date deficit is about $1.070T, now above 2025's record pace ($1.047T). Topping 2025's full-year record would take only about $80B a month in November and December, and the monthly deficit hasn't been that low since January.
▪️ Q4 GDP: October's gap was $20.8B above the Q3 monthly average, pointing to another drag from trade, partly offset by inventory builds (wholesale +0.9%, retail +0.8%, both the most since July).
▪️ Not inflation-adjusted, and AI hardware import prices have been rising, so the full report on December 8 will show how much of the jump is real volume.

Source: Census Bureau, BEA, Bloomberg.

Gavin Baker says Grok Bot feels like another ChatGPT moment because it turns hours of Claude Code work into seconds:

"You see these 23-year-old kids and just the way they use AI, they're just fluent and native in it. I just feel like maybe in a way that no matter how hard I try, I will never be, and I'm trying really hard."

"We got Claude Code. I built some stuff, did some cool stuff, and in, I don't know, 3 minutes of creating Grok Bots, I had much better versions of everything I created."

"I love having a podcast summarizer... It takes 10 seconds in Grok Bot. It's amazing, and it's so good."

"A Substack summarizer, an X summarizer, an X sentiment tracker for topics and stocks... All of those would have taken me hours working with Claude Code, and they each took 7 to 12 seconds with Grok Bot. And it's better."

"To me, Grok Bot does feel like another ChatGPT moment."

@GavinSBaker @DavidGeorge83

thread_tweets.text:
I have to use the official classification within bbg for 13F filers... Every single thing you mentioned is true but it is classified at the entity level. I get into this and the caveats in the writing of my notes. I am not going in and manually changing the classification for 2200 filers based on which part of an entity is most likely the primary holder of the asset. Bank of America is a Bank. Bbg is not going to change the filer type for BofA. A chunk of BofA isn't just their AP arm. it includes stuff held on behalf of client assets they manage. How much is from the AP and how much is from the clients? I have no idea. Same with pretty much every other filer on there. There are *HUGE* caveats with this data and even the filer level data is almost certainly best classified as "Multiple". Some entities break stuff out a bunch of different underlying entities. Others don't.  Wells has like 7 filers. BofA has 1. Citadel has 1. Would i love to know that breakout. yes. 

Do i? No.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
I have not got the last couple of months right, and I want to say that plainly.

Core inflation has surprised on the high side of my data, the energy shock lasted longer than I expected, and the book has paid for it. I own that.

But here is the thing about macro: EVERYTHING is a probability-weighted game. You put the odds on scenarios, you size for them, and then the world changes the odds on you. It happens all the time, and it will make you wrong from time to time. That is not a bug in the process. That is the process.

Anyone who tells you they avoid drawdowns, or that they are never wrong, is not worth listening to. They are either not taking risk, or not telling you the truth.

I don't have perma views. I am not a perma bull or a perma bear on anything. I let my own data guide me, the nowcasts I built to track growth, inflation and liquidity in real time, and our in-sample testing of them is very strong. The goal is not to be right every month. It is to be more right than wrong over time, and to know when the data has changed its mind before the market has.

Right now that data is telling me something very different from what the Fed was handed this week.

We give Real Vision members insights into these data sets DAILY. This week only, it's 60% off, the best chance of the year to get in 👇

This week's price action has made one thing pretty clear: the AI trade still has unresolved questions around Nvidia and where the money flows next. Until the market gets clarity on that, I would expect more of the volatility we saw on Wednesday.

$DELL posted strong earnings. $NVDA posted even stronger earnings, but the Huang drama has buried the numbers. Both stocks got sold anyway, because the recent selling comes from investors' fear of an AI bubble rather than from anything in the actual results. 

This reminds us that there is a disconnect between the financial performance of
these tech companies and the performance of their stock price.

The chop will continue until they both line up again.

The S&P 500 fell 11.6% from its October 6th record to its November 20th low.

Since 1963, there have been 19 declines of 10% or more.

Without a recession, the median decline was 17% and took 7 months to get back to a record.

With a recession, it was 36% and 39 months.

When a recession develops, drawdowns have a higher risk of cascading into bear markets.

Therefore, an important factor in medium-term stock market outcomes, while not infallible, is spotting recession risk.
